hints: Look at the three functional groups in X separately, the carboxylic acid, the alcohol, and the alkene, and ask which one each reagent actually attacks.
Remember that aqueous NaOH neutralises a carboxylic acid to a salt, but a typical secondary alcohol is far too weakly acidic to react with it.
Recall that LiAlH4 reduces a carboxylic acid all the way to a primary alcohol, but it leaves an isolated C=C double bond untouched.
walkthrough:
**Identify the functional groups in X**

Think of X as having three different parts to test. It has $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ (carboxylic acid), $\text{OH}$ (secondary alcohol), and a C=C double bond in the ring.

$$\text{X = cyclohexene with CO}_2\text{H + OH}$$

**Form Y from NaOH(aq)**

NaOH is a base that neutralises acids. Carboxylic acids react easily to give the sodium salt plus water, but alcohols do not react with aqueous NaOH.

$$\text{RCO}_2\text{H + NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na + H}_2\text{O}$$

**Form Z from LiAlH4**

LiAlH4 is a strong reducing agent. It reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol, $\text{CO}_2\text{H} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, but it does not reduce an isolated alkene.

$$\text{RCO}_2\text{H} \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} \text{RCH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Check what stays the same**

In both reactions the ring C=C and the secondary $\text{OH}$ group are unchanged. So Y keeps $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ with $\text{OH}$, and Z keeps $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ with $\text{OH}$, both still unsaturated.

options.A: Correct. Y shows only the acid neutralised to $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ while the alcohol and C=C remain, and Z shows only the acid reduced to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ while the alcohol and C=C remain. This matches the selective chemistry perfectly.
options.B: Y is right but Z is wrong. Z still shows $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and the double bond has disappeared. This comes from the trap that LiAlH4 reduces C=C, but LiAlH4 does not reduce an isolated alkene, it only reduces the carboxylic acid to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.
options.C: Z is right but Y is wrong. Y shows $\text{ONa}$ as well as $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$. This comes from thinking the alcohol reacts with NaOH like a phenol does, but a secondary alcohol is not acidic enough to react with aqueous NaOH.
options.D: Both parts are wrong in detail. Y wrongly shows the alcohol converted to $\text{ONa}$, and Z wrongly shows no reduction of the acid and loss of the C=C. It combines both misconceptions about NaOH reacting with alcohols and LiAlH4 reducing alkenes.
